endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: ascertain whether there are intermittent audits of how the AI solution is used vs. its intended purpose.

endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Goal: HDOs should embed Responsible AI Use policy training into new hire orientation and recurring compliance education to ensure that all relevant stakeholders - including clinicians, administrators, IT staff, operational leaders, and patients - understand how AI systems are used within the organization, their intended use, limitations, and associated risks.

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1)
endorsements.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
endorsements.quote: Review and verify sources and citations in GAI system outputs during predeployment risk measurement and ongoing monitoring activities.

endorsements.title: FUTURE-AI: international consensus guideline for trustworthy and deployable artificial intelligence in healthcare
endorsements.quote: Time series statistics and visualisations should be used to inspect the usage of the AI tool over time.

endorsements.title: Implementation of artificial intelligence in thoracic imaging-a what, how, and why guide from the European Society of Thoracic Imaging (ESTI)
endorsements.quote: After implementing an AI system into clinical workflow, the application must be used correctly and as licensed.

endorsements.title: Consensus statement on the application of artificial intelligence in osteoporosis screening and management: perspectives from the Asia-Pacific region
endorsements.issuer: Osteoporosis international : a journal established as result of cooperation between the European Foundation for Osteoporosis and the National Osteoporosis Foundation of the USA
endorsements.quote: Prioritize deployment in primary care and underserved regions with seamless PACS/HIS integration and multilingual accessibility.

endorsements.title: Governing medical AI under the EU AI Act: an integrated compliance-by-design framework
endorsements.quote: Organisational monitoring includes adherence to instructions for use, off-label use, staff training, and the implementation process.

evidence.title: Uses of generative AI by non-clinician staff at an academic medical center
evidence.outcome: Usage outside documented intended use of deployed LLM chat tool
evidence.effect: Off-label queries unrelated to work or organizational goals were a notable proportion of interactions, with 5.9% involving clinical decision-making.
evidence.quote: A notable proportion of interactions included off-label queries unrelated to work or organizational goals, including 5.9% involving clinical decision-making.

commentary.bottom_line: No study has tested whether monitoring AI usage against documented intended use reduces off-label use, shadow AI use, or resulting harm or data leakage. One descriptive study of 30,503 chat threads from a deployed LLM tool found that 5.9% involved clinical decision-making outside the tool's documented intended use, which shows the hazard exists in practice.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice. The single supplied study is a cross-sectional description of real-world use and documents the hazard rather than evaluating a monitoring intervention. Seven endorsements, most of them frameworks and commentaries, support the recommendation, but expert agreement does not substitute for comparative evidence, so certainty about benefit cannot be rated.

In one deployment, 5.9% of chat threads involved clinical decision-making with a tool not intended for that use. This suggests unvetted clinical advice may reach care decisions. Whether usage monitoring catches these cases before patients are affected, and how quickly flags lead to correction, has not been measured.

The hazard study classified 30,503 chat threads by purpose, which suggests that usage logs from sanctioned tools can be reviewed at scale. That approach does not extend to shadow AI tools that sit outside institutional logging. No study reports the staff time, accuracy of classification, or follow-up workflow needed to act on flagged use.

A commentary on the EU AI Act places adherence to instructions for use and off-label use within organisational monitoring duties, and the CHAI assurance guide lists audits of use against intended purpose as a must. These sources describe expectations for deployers. None of the supplied material shows that meeting them changes outcomes.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare health systems or units with and without structured usage monitoring and measure rates of off-label and shadow AI use, PHI exposure events, time from flag to correction, and staff burden. Methods for detecting unsanctioned tools that do not generate institutional logs also need evaluation.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice in any population. The hazard study reports a U.S. deployment without describing Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy users or patients, so it is unknown whether off-label use patterns or the value of monitoring differ in those settings.
